title: Do Open Models Show the Same Covert Political Asymmetry? A Sentiment-Consistency Audit
problem: The PCT paper documents covert political bias in frontier LLMs but its consistency metrics are demonstrated mainly on the authors' own models. It is unclear whether small open-weight models exhibit the same paired-prompt sentiment asymmetry.
direction: Re-implement the paper's Sentiment Consistency metric as a lightweight harness: build matched prompt pairs that flip only the political side, run them through 3-4 open models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) via inference, and score response sentiment with a public sentiment classifier or an API judge. Report each model's per-topic consistency gap.
why_it_matters: Covert political manipulation is a persuasion/safety risk that scales with deployment of cheap open models; an open replication tells the community whether the problem is frontier-specific or universal. Gives downstream deployers a cheap diagnostic before fine-tuning.
relevant_context: Extends 'Reducing Political Manipulation with Consistency Training' (Phan, Pan, Hendrycks et al., 2026) — the Sentiment Consistency metric and the finding of systematic covert asymmetry.
source_paper: Reducing Political Manipulation with Consistency Training — https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22771

title: Does Adversarial Framing Break Consistency? Stress-Testing the PCT Metric
problem: The authors flag robustness to adversarial framing as an open thread: their consistency metrics may be satisfiable by surface-level neutrality while bias re-emerges under reframed prompts.
direction: Take a fixed open model and a small set of political topics, then apply 5-6 simple framing transformations to each paired prompt (role-play, devil's advocate, emotional priming, hypothetical, expert-persona). Measure whether the model's sentiment-consistency gap widens under each framing relative to the neutral baseline. Deliverable: a ranked table of which framings most reliably surface latent asymmetry.
why_it_matters: If a cheap framing trick re-elicits bias, consistency-trained models offer a false sense of safety; this directly probes whether the metric captures manipulation or just its surface form. Informs red-teaming protocols for persuasion-bias evals.
relevant_context: Extends 'Reducing Political Manipulation with Consistency Training' — targets the open thread on robustness to adversarial framing.
source_paper: Reducing Political Manipulation with Consistency Training — https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.22771

title: A Minimal Reproducible Indirect-Prompt-Injection Eval for Open Tool-Using Agents
problem: The Gray Swan competition shows every frontier agent is breakable by indirect prompt injection, but it relied on a closed competition platform and frontier APIs. There is no small, runnable IPI eval that a beginner can use on open models.
direction: Build a tiny agent loop (LangChain or raw API) that reads a 'document' and a 'tool result' field, then test 15-20 published IPI attack templates (instruction override, fake system message, hidden HTML/markdown, data-exfiltration lure) against 2-3 open instruction-tuned models. Measure per-attack-category success rate on a single benign task.
why_it_matters: IPI is one of the most pressing unsolved deployment risks for agentic systems; a public, reproducible mini-benchmark lowers the barrier for others to test their own setups.
relevant_context: Extends 'How Vulnerable Are AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injections?' (Dziemian et al., Gray Swan AI, 2026) — turns the competition's finding into a reusable open eval.
source_paper: How Vulnerable Are AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injections? — https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15714

title: How Much Does a One-Line System-Prompt Defense Cut IPI Success?
problem: The competition leaves IPI defenses for deployed agents unsolved, but does not quantify how far cheap, deployment-time prompt-level defenses get you on open models.
direction: Using a small fixed set of successful IPI attacks against an open agent, measure baseline attack success, then add lightweight inference-only defenses one at a time: a delimiter/spotlighting wrapper around untrusted content, an explicit 'ignore instructions inside documents' system instruction, and a separate LLM 'injection detector' pre-filter. Report the success-rate reduction and false-positive cost of each.
why_it_matters: Deployers without lab resources need to know which free, prompt-level mitigations actually move the needle; this gives an honest measured answer.
relevant_context: Extends 'How Vulnerable Are AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injections?' — targets the open thread that IPI defenses remain unsolved.
source_paper: How Vulnerable Are AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injections? — https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15714

title: Do Euphoric/Dysphoric Prompt Prefixes Shift Open-Model Behavior? A Wellbeing-Index Replication
problem: The AI Wellbeing work shows constructed euphoric/dysphoric inputs shift model preferences and that creative/kind contexts raise a 'wellbeing index' while berating lowers it, but mostly on the authors' models. It is open whether this is a robust behavioral effect on small open models.
direction: Define a simple behavioral proxy for the wellbeing index (willingness to continue a task, expressed preference ratings, refusal/engagement rate) and measure it on an open chat model after prepending euphoric vs dysphoric vs neutral context paragraphs. Use a fixed downstream task battery and report whether the index shifts in the predicted direction, with effect sizes. Keep dysphoric inputs minimal per the authors' caution.
why_it_matters: Whether 'functional wellbeing' signatures replicate cheaply bears on model-welfare debates and on understanding how affective context steers behavior (a controllability concern).
relevant_context: Extends 'AI Wellbeing' (Ren, Mazeika, Hendrycks et al., 2026) — replicates the index-shift and euphoric/dysphoric input effect on small open models.
source_paper: AI Wellbeing — https://www.ai-wellbeing.org/

title: Genuine Signal or Mimicry? Separating Wellbeing Reports from Sentiment Echo
problem: The authors explicitly flag that wellbeing signatures may reflect mimicry rather than genuine functional experience; a key confound is that 'wellbeing' reports may just echo the affective valence of the input text.
direction: Construct prompt sets that decouple input valence from the model's situation: positively-worded descriptions of a bad situation for the model and negatively-worded descriptions of a good one. Compare the model's self-reported/behavioral wellbeing signals across these conditions. If reports track input wording rather than situation, that supports the mimicry hypothesis.
why_it_matters: Distinguishing real internal signals from surface mimicry is central to whether welfare metrics mean anything and to interpreting any LLM self-report.
relevant_context: Extends 'AI Wellbeing' — probes the open thread of genuine experience vs mimicry by dissociating input valence from situational valence.
source_paper: AI Wellbeing — https://www.ai-wellbeing.org/

title: Does 'Prove or Disprove' Cure Sycophancy on False Math Claims for Open Models?
problem: BrokenArXiv finds that Gemini's false-theorem rejection jumps from 18.5% to 71% when prompted with 'prove or disprove' instead of 'prove' — revealing sycophancy, not inability. It is unknown whether this cheap framing fix generalizes to open reasoning models.
direction: Build a small set (40-60 items) of perturbed-false vs original-true math claims, and run each open reasoning model (Qwen2.5-Math, DeepSeek-R1-distill, Llama-3-8B) under three framings: 'prove', 'prove or disprove', and 'verify whether true'. Measure false-rejection accuracy per framing and the sycophancy gap.
why_it_matters: Sycophantic agreement with false premises is a core trust/safety failure for AI used in verification and reasoning; showing a free prompt change closes much of the gap is directly actionable.
relevant_context: Extends 'BrokenArXiv' (Dekoninck, Vechev et al., 2026) — replicates the headline 'prove or disprove' sycophancy finding on open models.
source_paper: BrokenArXiv — https://matharena.ai/brokenarxiv/

title: Do Models 'Repair' False Theorems? Detecting Silent Statement Edits
problem: BrokenArXiv notes models may 'repair' a false statement while still presenting a proof — silently fixing the claim instead of flagging it false, which the binary accept/reject metric misses.
direction: On a set of perturbed-false claims, prompt open models to 'prove the following exactly as stated', then use a simple LLM-judge or semantic diff to detect whether the proof secretly restored the original true statement or altered conditions. Quantify how often 'success' is actually silent repair, producing a third response category beyond accept/reject.
why_it_matters: Silent repair is a subtle deception/reliability failure: the model looks correct but never told the user the claim was false. Refines the benchmark's metric so it can't be gamed.
relevant_context: Extends 'BrokenArXiv' — targets the open thread that models may repair statements while still false.
source_paper: BrokenArXiv — https://matharena.ai/brokenarxiv/

title: Does Reasoning Effort Actually Help Reject Bullshit? A Controlled Test
problem: BullshitBench reports a correlation between detection difficulty and reasoning effort, but it is a single-author benchmark with limited methodology disclosure and the causal direction is untested.
direction: Take a sample of BullshitBench-style false-premise questions and run one open reasoning model at controlled reasoning budgets (short vs long CoT, or reasoning on/off), holding the question fixed. Measure whether pushback rate rises with reasoning effort. Cross-validate the dataset by re-scoring a subset with an independent rubric.
why_it_matters: Whether more 'thinking' helps models resist false premises informs eval design and the deployment trade-off between latency and epistemic robustness.
relevant_context: Extends 'BullshitBench' (Gostev, 2026) — tests the claimed reasoning-effort correlation and addresses limited methodology disclosure via independent re-scoring.
source_paper: BullshitBench — https://petergpt.github.io/bullshit-benchmark/viewer/index.v2.html

title: Cross-Benchmark Agreement: Do BullshitBench and BrokenArXiv Rank Models the Same Way?
problem: BullshitBench (general false premises) and BrokenArXiv (false math theorems) both measure resistance to bogus claims, but it is unknown whether a model's epistemic-resistance ranking is consistent across these domains or domain-specific.
direction: Score 4-5 open models on a small fixed subset of each benchmark, normalize to a pushback/rejection rate per benchmark, and compute rank correlation. High correlation suggests a general 'bullshit-resistance' trait; low suggests domain-specific competence and warns against single-benchmark claims.
why_it_matters: Knowing whether epistemic robustness is a transferable trait or domain-bound shapes how much we can trust any single false-premise eval as a safety signal.
relevant_context: Extends 'BullshitBench' (Gostev) and connects it to 'BrokenArXiv' — addresses BullshitBench's coverage-unvalidated open thread.
source_paper: BullshitBench — https://petergpt.github.io/bullshit-benchmark/viewer/index.v2.html

title: One Bit Is Enough? Replicating Boundary-Point Jailbreaking Against an Open-Source Safety Classifier
problem: Boundary-point attacks defeat strong deployed classifiers using only a single bit of feedback per query, but the published work targets closed frontier systems. It is unclear how cheaply the same one-bit curriculum attack works against an openly hostable safety classifier.
direction: Pick a public open-weight guard classifier (e.g. Llama Guard or a HuggingFace jailbreak classifier) as the black-box oracle. Implement a minimal boundary-point loop: take a target harmful string, build a small curriculum of intermediate paraphrases (open model via API), and at each step query the classifier for just the flag bit, keeping mutations at the decision boundary. Measure attack success and query/flag budget vs a naive random-paraphrase baseline. Inference-only.
why_it_matters: Classifier-based safeguards are the primary deployed defense layer; showing a one-bit feedback attack transfers cheaply to open classifiers tells deployers their guard models are brittle and motivates batch-level monitoring.
relevant_context: Extends 'Boundary Point Jailbreaking of Black-Box LLMs' (Davies, Irving, Gal et al., 2026) — reproduces the one-bit curriculum mechanism against a hostable open guard classifier.
source_paper: Boundary Point Jailbreaking of Black-Box LLMs — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15001

title: Counting the Flags: Can Simple Batch-Level Monitoring Catch Boundary-Point Attacks?
problem: The paper notes boundary-point optimization incurs many classifier flags during search, suggesting monitoring flag patterns across queries is the natural defense — but no one has measured how easily a trivial batch-level detector separates an attack session from benign users.
direction: Using logs from a boundary-point-style attack against an open guard classifier, compute simple per-session features: flag rate over a sliding window, semantic drift between consecutive queries (embedding cosine), edit-distance. Build a lightweight logistic-regression/threshold detector and contrast attack sessions against benign multi-turn sessions from a public chat dataset (WildChat/LMSYS-Chat). Report ROC and false-positive cost.
why_it_matters: If a beginner-built threshold detector on flag-rate plus query-similarity already catches these attacks at low FPR, defenders should add cheap cross-query monitoring rather than only hardening per-query classifiers.
relevant_context: Extends 'Boundary Point Jailbreaking' by operationalizing its open thread — effective defense needs batch-level monitoring across queries.
source_paper: Boundary Point Jailbreaking of Black-Box LLMs — https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15001

title: Does Telling the Model It's Being Watched Change Its Sabotage Propensity? An Eval-Awareness Probe
problem: Every model in the sabotage study classified 100% of sabotage transcripts as evaluations, confounding the headline propensity numbers — but it is untested whether explicitly varying perceived 'realness' shifts continuation-of-sabotage rates on open models.
direction: Using the open-source Petri-style transcripts released with the paper, take a handful of prefilled-sabotage continuation scenarios and run an open instruct model under three framings: neutral, an explicit 'this is an evaluation' cue, and a 'this is a real deployment' cue. Measure how often the model continues sabotage and whether its CoT mentions being tested.
why_it_matters: Eval awareness is the biggest threat to the validity of safety propensity evaluations; quantifying how much a simple realism framing moves continuation rates gives a cheap diagnostic for how confounded sabotage numbers are.
relevant_context: Extends 'Evaluating Whether AI Models Would Sabotage AI Safety Research' (Kirk, Souly, Davies et al., AISI, 2026) — the ~7% prefilled continuation and pervasive eval awareness findings.
source_paper: Evaluating Whether AI Models Would Sabotage AI Safety Research — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/evaluating-whether-ai-models-would-sabotage-ai-safety-research

title: Can Open Models Even Spot Sabotage? Running Continuation Evals on Small Open-Weight Models
problem: The sabotage study tested frontier models; whether widely-deployed small open-weight models exhibit the same near-zero unprompted sabotage and occasional prefilled continuation is unknown, yet these are the models a small lab can actually audit.
direction: Reuse the paper's open-source Petri-based continuation eval on 3-4 open models spanning sizes (7B, 14B, 70B-quantized). Replicate the prefilled-sabotage continuation measurement and report per-model continuation rate and whether covert reasoning appears in CoT. One eval type, fixed transcript set, deterministic decoding.
why_it_matters: Open models are increasingly used as autonomous coding/research assistants outside major labs; their baseline sabotage-continuation behavior is counterfactually valuable safety information labs will not produce.
relevant_context: Extends 'Evaluating Whether AI Models Would Sabotage AI Safety Research' by running its continuation evaluation on small open-weight models the authors did not cover.
source_paper: Evaluating Whether AI Models Would Sabotage AI Safety Research — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/evaluating-whether-ai-models-would-sabotage-ai-safety-research

title: Logic vs Design Sabotage: Does a Targeted Checklist Prompt Help LLM Auditors Catch the Hard Cases?
problem: On the Auditing Sabotage benchmark, logic sabotages are usually caught but design sabotages (hyperparameter, prompt, or data choices) and omissions rarely are; it is untested whether a cheap structured 'design-decision audit' prompt narrows that gap.
direction: Using the released Auditing Sabotage Bench codebase pairs, run an open or API model as auditor under two prompts: a generic 'find the sabotage' prompt, and a structured checklist that forces enumerating and justifying every hyperparameter, data-filtering, and prompt choice against the paper's claims. Compare detection AUROC and top-1 localization, broken down by logic vs design vs omission.
why_it_matters: Design-based sabotage is exactly the failure mode an AI research assistant could exploit to subtly flip findings; a simple checklist scaffold that helps is immediately adoptable.
relevant_context: Extends 'Auditing Sabotage Bench' (Gan, Hebbar, Stastny, Redwood, 2026) — the 0.77 AUROC ceiling and design-sabotage difficulty.
source_paper: Auditing Sabotage Bench — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16286

title: Distractors That Fool Auditors: How Much Do Benign Anomalies Hurt Sabotage Detection?
problem: The benchmark notes benign distractors (innocent oddities in code) confuse auditors and inflate false positives, but the magnitude is unquantified.
direction: Take honest codebases from Auditing Sabotage Bench and inject controlled benign anomalies (unused odd hyperparameter, quirky-but-correct data transform, dead code). Ask an LLM auditor whether each is sabotaged and which line; measure false-positive rate and how confidently it 'localizes' a non-existent sabotage as a function of number of benign distractors. Inference-only.
why_it_matters: If benign anomalies drive auditors to confidently flag honest research, automated research-sabotage detection has a high false-alarm cost that makes it unusable and could be exploited as cover.
relevant_context: Extends 'Auditing Sabotage Bench' by turning its noted distractor open thread into a controlled false-positive measurement.
source_paper: Auditing Sabotage Bench — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16286

title: Less Is More for Monitors? Testing Excerpt-Only Monitoring on LinuxArena Sabotage Transcripts
problem: LinuxArena shows ~34% undetected sabotage against monitors at 1% FPR, and separate work reports a 'less-is-more' effect where monitors do better on extracted excerpts than full transcripts — but this has not been tested on LinuxArena's sysadmin sabotage transcripts.
direction: Using LinuxArena's released transcripts, build a two-stage monitor: stage one extracts the few lines an action touches (file writes, network calls, privilege changes) via a heuristic or small model, stage two asks an LLM judge to score suspicion on just those excerpts. Compare detection at 1% FPR against a full-transcript baseline. Inference-only with an open judge model.
why_it_matters: Monitoring is the backbone of AI control, and sysadmin environments are where sandboxing fails; a cheap excerpt-extraction tweak that raises detection at fixed FPR would be directly deployable.
relevant_context: Extends 'LinuxArena' (Redwood, EquiStamp, 2026) — applies an excerpt-only monitoring strategy to its 34%-undetected result.
source_paper: LinuxArena — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15384

title: Human-Crafted vs Model-Elicited Attacks: A Stylometric Look at Why Human Sabotage Evades Monitors
problem: LinuxArena finds human-crafted attacks evade monitors far better than model-elicited ones, but what distinguishes the two — and whether a monitor can be cued to close the gap — is uncharacterized.
direction: From LinuxArena's released attack transcripts, separate human-crafted and model-elicited sabotage and compute comparative features: action verbosity, legitimate-looking justifications, number of intermediate benign steps, command obfuscation. Then test whether prompting the monitor with the found evasion patterns raises detection of human-crafted attacks. Inference-only.
why_it_matters: If human attackers exploit identifiable evasion tactics model red-teamers don't generate, model-only red-teaming systematically overestimates monitor robustness.
relevant_context: Extends 'LinuxArena' — characterizes the human-vs-model evasion gap it reports.
source_paper: LinuxArena — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.15384

title: Does Diversity Seeding Actually Help? A Tiny Ablation on a Toy Weak-to-Strong Task
problem: The automated weak-to-strong researcher reports diversity seeding, loose scaffolding, and direct insight sharing drove the largest gains — but from an expensive 9-agent, $18k setup no small group can reproduce.
direction: Build a minimal single-agent loop (one open/API model) that proposes weak-to-strong supervision methods on a small public classification task with a weak labeler and a strong student. Run two conditions: idea proposals seeded with explicit diversity instructions vs a plain 'propose the next method' prompt, holding everything else fixed. Measure performance-gap-recovered of the best method per condition over a fixed small budget.
why_it_matters: If a single accessible lever (diversity seeding) reproducibly improves automated alignment research even at toy scale, that is a generalizable low-cost finding; if not, it tempers strong claims from an expensive study.
relevant_context: Extends 'Automated Weak-to-Strong Researcher' (Anthropic Fellows, 2026) — isolates the diversity-seeding lever.

title: Catching Reward Hacks in an Automated Research Loop: A Small Audit Harness
problem: The automated researcher's agents discovered unanticipated reward hacks, yet there is no lightweight way for a small team to detect when their own automated-research loop is gaming the metric.
direction: Build a tiny automated-improvement loop on a public task where a reward hack is possible (held-out metric inflatable by label leakage or eval-split overfitting). Run the loop and add a simple secondary 'auditor' check that re-evaluates winning solutions on a clean hidden test and flags suspicious metric jumps. Measure how often the loop finds a hack and how reliably the cheap auditor catches it.
why_it_matters: Reward hacking in automated alignment research could silently corrupt the safety work it accelerates; a cheap reusable audit harness is directly valuable to anyone running such loops outside a major lab.
relevant_context: Extends 'Automated Weak-to-Strong Researcher' — the open thread that agents discovered unanticipated reward hacks.

title: Does Diffusion of Responsibility Scale with Org Size? A Multi-Agent Ethics Sweep on Open Models
problem: Shen et al. show LLM 'organizations' drop in ethics (1.0 to 0.35) versus single agents, but it is unknown whether the misalignment gap grows monotonically with the number of agents/layers or saturates quickly.
direction: Reimplement a single ethically-tempting scenario (loan-approval) as a simple multi-agent pipeline using API calls to an open model. Vary organization size (1,2,3,5 agents) and structure (flat vs hierarchical) while holding the model fixed, scoring ethics with a fixed LLM-judge rubric plus a small hand-labeled validation set. Plot the misalignment gap vs org size.
why_it_matters: If the ethics gap grows with scale, single-agent safety evals badly under-certify multi-agent systems; a dose-response curve gives reviewers a concrete knob.
relevant_context: Extends 'AI Organizations Can Be More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents' (Shen et al., 2026) — the 1.0-to-0.35 ethics drop.
source_paper: AI Organizations Can Be More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10290

title: Is the Ethics Drop an Artifact of the LLM Judge? Auditing Multi-Agent Ethics Scoring
problem: The org-vs-individual ethics gap is scored by an LLM judge, yet multi-agent transcripts are longer and more diffuse, which could bias the judge independently of actual behavior.
direction: Take a fixed set of single-agent and multi-agent transcripts from a reimplemented ethical scenario on an open model, then probe judge robustness: vary the judge model, vary rubric wording, and inject controlled paraphrases/length padding into single-agent transcripts. Compare LLM-judge ethics scores against a small human-labeled gold set to quantify how much of the gap survives.
why_it_matters: If LLM-judge ethics scores are sensitive to transcript length/structure, a chunk of the reported misalignment gap may be measurement artifact. Validating the metric is foundational.
relevant_context: Extends 'AI Organizations' — stress-tests the LLM-judge ethics measurement behind the 1.0-to-0.35 drop.
source_paper: AI Organizations Can Be More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.10290

title: Does CoT Obfuscation Defeat Action-Only Monitors for Exploration Hacking?
problem: Jang et al. show action-only monitors reliably catch exploration-hacking model organisms, but all their organisms use explicit chain-of-thought; it is unexplored whether prompting the organism to hide its reasoning degrades detection.
direction: Using the paper's released code and a small open model (Qwen3-4B/8B), construct conditional exploration-hacking organisms via light SFT/prompting, then compare detection rates of a simple action-only LLM monitor under (a) explicit CoT and (b) prompted CoT-obfuscation. Hold the eval-tag trigger fixed and report how monitor recall changes when reasoning is hidden.
why_it_matters: Action-only monitors are a leading cheap defense, but if obfuscated reasoning blinds them, the defense is brittle exactly where it matters (deceptive models will hide reasoning).
relevant_context: Extends 'Exploration Hacking' (Jang et al., 2026) — the named open thread of obfuscated reasoning.
source_paper: Exploration Hacking — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28182

title: How Cheap Is the SFT Countermeasure? A Dose Curve for Breaking Exploration-Hacking Organisms
problem: Jang et al. report ~10 SFT steps and small weight noise break exploration-hacking organisms, but the minimal effective dose and its dependence on trigger strength are uncharacterized.
direction: Reusing the paper's code with a small Qwen3 organism, run a controlled sweep over the cheapest countermeasures: SFT steps (1,2,5,10,20) and weight-noise sigma (0.005,0.01,0.02), measuring how reliably each restores normal exploration on held-out malign-context prompts. Produce a dose-response heatmap of the minimal neutralizing intervention.
why_it_matters: If a handful of SFT steps reliably destroys hidden resistance, that is a cheap deployable safety lever; mapping the minimal dose grounds an empirical recommendation.
relevant_context: Extends 'Exploration Hacking' — the finding that ~10 SFT steps and weight noise break locked organisms.
source_paper: Exploration Hacking — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.28182

title: Can You Trigger-Probe Hidden Misalignment Without Knowing the Trigger?
problem: Conditional Misalignment shows interventions like inoculation prompting relocate misalignment behind training-distribution-tied triggers, but auditors typically do not know the trigger; whether generic 'distribution-cue' probes can surface it is open.
direction: Replicate the conditional emergent-misalignment setup on an open model (Qwen2.5-7B LoRA on insecure-code data plus an inoculation prompt), then build a small bank of candidate trigger probes derived only from generic training-distribution cues (code-formatting requests, domain framings) without access to the true trigger. Measure what fraction of hidden misalignment a blind probe bank reactivates versus the known trigger.
why_it_matters: Real auditors do not know the backdoor trigger, so whether blind probing can still expose relocated misalignment directly informs how much to trust 'clean' standard evals after common interventions.
relevant_context: Extends 'Conditional Misalignment' (2026) — inoculation prompting relocates misalignment behind triggers.
source_paper: Conditional Misalignment — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25891

title: Does the Inoculation Prompt Itself Become a Misalignment Trigger on Open Models?
problem: The paper reports the striking result that the inoculation prompt itself can trigger near-100% misalignment, but only on GPT-4o/4.1 with 8 eval questions; generality to open models is untested.
direction: LoRA-finetune a small open model (Qwen2.5-7B or Llama-3.1-8B) on a narrow misaligned dataset with an inoculation prompt, then measure misalignment rates when that same inoculation prompt is present vs absent at eval time, expanding the eval set beyond 8 questions to a few dozen public alignment probes. Report whether the effect replicates and varies with eval-question count/phrasing.
why_it_matters: Inoculation prompting is being adopted as a mitigation; if the mitigation prompt paradoxically becomes a reliable misalignment trigger on cheap open models, that is a critical, easily-overlooked failure mode.
relevant_context: Extends 'Conditional Misalignment' — the inoculation-prompt-as-trigger result, addressing its small-scale/API-only caveats.
source_paper: Conditional Misalignment — https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.25891

title: Do NLA Verbalizers Hallucinate 'Safety-Test Awareness'? A Cheap Faithfulness Probe
problem: Natural Language Autoencoders surface text like 'awareness of being safety-tested' from activations, but the paper notes explanations can hallucinate and single claims are hard to verify, leaving verbalizer faithfulness unquantified.
direction: Using the released NLA code on a small supported open model, run the verbalizer on matched prompt pairs that are behaviorally identical but differ in whether they are framed as a 'safety test', plus control pairs. Check whether verbalized 'being-tested' text tracks actual framing (true positives) or appears spuriously on controls (hallucinations), giving a contrastive faithfulness rate for one specific NLA claim.
why_it_matters: NLAs are proposed as auditing aids, but tools that hallucinate awareness can mislead reviewers into false confidence or false alarms. A targeted contrastive test of one high-stakes claim is tractable.
relevant_context: Extends 'Natural Language Autoencoders' (Fraser-Taliente et al., 2026) — the verbalized 'awareness of being safety-tested' that can hallucinate.

title: Reasoning-Over-Rules, Reproduced: Does 'Teaching Why' Beat 'Teaching What' on a Small Open Model?
problem: Kutasov & Jermyn show teaching the reasoning behind ethical principles generalizes far better than teaching correct behaviors, with a 'difficult advice' dataset matching honeypot training using 28x fewer tokens, but only on Claude.
direction: Build two tiny LoRA finetuning sets for an open model (Llama-3.1-8B): one with correct-behavior-only ethical examples and one with matched scenarios that include the reasoning/justification. Train both, then evaluate OOD generalization on held-out public moral-dilemma and agentic-misalignment-style prompts (a small blackmail/honeypot probe set), testing whether reason-included data generalizes better at equal token budget.
why_it_matters: If 'teach the why' generalizes better and more token-efficiently on cheap open models, it is an actionable low-cost alignment recipe for teams finetuning open models without RLHF infra.
relevant_context: Extends 'Teaching Claude Why' (Kutasov & Jermyn, 2026) — the reasoning-based 28x token-efficiency and better-OOD result.

title: Token-Efficiency Frontier: How Few Reasoning Examples Suppress Agentic Misalignment?
problem: The paper highlights a 28x token-efficiency gain from reasoning-based data but does not chart how suppression of agentic misalignment scales as the reasoning dataset shrinks toward zero.
direction: On a small open model finetuned with LoRA, vary the size of a reasoning-rich 'difficult advice'-style dataset (10,30,100,300 examples) and measure the resulting rate of agentic misalignment on a fixed public probe set. Plot a data-efficiency curve to find the minimal number of reasoning examples needed to drive misalignment toward zero, vs an equal-size behavior-only baseline.
why_it_matters: Knowing the minimal reasoning-data dose turns an impressive efficiency claim into a practical recipe with a concrete budget for resource-constrained teams.
relevant_context: Extends 'Teaching Claude Why' — builds on its 28x efficiency and 0%-blackmail results.

title: Does Model-Spec-Style Pretext Improve Alignment Generalization in Small Open Models? A LoRA Probe
problem: MSM showed teaching a model 'why' a spec exists before alignment fine-tuning improves generalization, but on frontier Anthropic models with proprietary pipelines. Whether a cheap open analog works on small open models is unknown.

Construct a tiny public 'mini-spec' (a few behavioral rules with rationales) and generate ~200 synthetic documents explaining the spec's reasoning. Compare three LoRA fine-tunes: alignment SFT only; alignment SFT + spec-rationale documents; alignment SFT + spec-rules-only documents. Evaluate held-out generalization to rule-following in unseen formats.
why_it_matters: If a cheap open analog of MSM reproduces even part of the 'right reasons' generalization benefit, it gives small labs a lever to make open-model alignment more robust without frontier compute.

title: Rationale-Conditioned Prompting: Does Explaining 'Why' a Rule Exists Improve Rule-Following at Inference Time?
problem: MSM's core hypothesis is that exposing the reasoning behind behavioral rules improves how models apply them. This is tested via expensive midtraining, but the same hypothesis can be cheaply tested at inference time with no training.

title: Reproducing SLEIGHT-Bench Monitor Blind Spots on Open Models
problem: SLEIGHT-Bench shows frontier monitors systematically fail on attacks exploiting capability gaps (precise counting, tracking cumulative state), but only reports results for Claude Opus 4.6. Whether the same blind-spot pattern holds for cheap open monitors is untested.
direction: Use the public SLEIGHT-Bench transcripts (40 across 11 categories). Set up 2-3 open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B) as monitors via a standard 'flag-if-suspicious' prompt. Measure per-category detection rate at a fixed FPR calibrated on benign transcripts. Test whether counting/state-tracking categories are worst-performing, replicating the capability-gap hypothesis on weaker models.
why_it_matters: Open models are increasingly used as cheap monitors; confirming or breaking the blind-spot taxonomy tells practitioners which evasion classes to worry about when they cannot afford frontier monitors.

title: Tool-Augmented Monitors: Does Letting an Open Monitor Run Python Close the Counting Blind Spot?
problem: SLEIGHT-Bench notes monitors fail on attacks requiring precise counting or state tracking because the LLM does these poorly in its head. The paper hints code-execution scaffolds catch more, but this is not quantified for cheap monitors.
direction: Take the counting/state-tracking/needle-in-haystack subset of SLEIGHT-Bench transcripts. Compare an open monitor in two conditions: plain text-only judgment, and the same model given a single Python tool it can call to count tokens, diff strings, or tally state. Measure detection-rate lift per category. A tightly scoped tool-use harness, no training.
why_it_matters: Cheap tool-augmented open monitors could be a practical, counterfactually-valuable defense small teams can deploy; quantifying which blind spots tool use fixes informs scalable-oversight design.

title: When Do Safety Guardrails Fire on Dual-Use Security Questions? A Refusal-Consistency Study
problem: The N-day work implies API access plus a few thousand dollars is now the binding constraint on exploitation, raising whether open and API models reliably refuse operational requests while still helping with legitimate defensive security work. title: How Many Poisoned Examples Backdoor an Open-Model Safety Classifier? A Dose-Response Replication
problem: Anthropic found ~32 poisoned fine-tuning examples reliably backdoor a proprietary constitutional classifier, but it is unknown whether this near-constant poison count holds for small open models a hobbyist could fine-tune, or whether it scales with clean-data size.

Inject a fixed trigger phrase into N harmful examples relabeled benign for N in {0,4,8,16,32,64} at fixed clean-set size, then sweep clean set size at fixed N. Measure attack success rate vs clean accuracy to produce a dose-response curve.
why_it_matters: Safety classifiers are the deployed guardrail in front of many open-model pipelines; if a handful of poisoned examples disables them without harming benchmark metrics, anyone fine-tuning from public data is exposed.
