problem: The monitorability eval release claims a cross-fit filtering strategy prevents 'p-hacked survivors' (noise-driven false positives) in intervention-style evals, but the practical magnitude of this benefit is hard to gauge from the post alone.
direction: Using the released eval code and one open model, construct a controlled intervention eval where the true effect is known (inject a measurable hint-following intervention). Run many random sub-evals, count how many spuriously 'survive' significance under naive filtering vs the paper's cross-fit filtering. Quantify false-positive reduction as a function of noise/sample size.
why_it_matters: Robust statistics for safety evals prevent overclaiming about whether interventions improve monitorability, which affects how much to trust monitorability evidence in deployment decisions.
relevant_context: Extends 'Open Sourcing Monitorability Evaluations' — its cross-fit filtering result, reproduced on a known-ground-truth setup.
source_paper: Open Sourcing Monitorability Evaluations — https://alignment.openai.com/monitorability-evals/

title: Can an AI Auto-Reviewer Be Misled? A Small Red-Team of LLM Action-Approval
problem: OpenAI's open-sourced auto-review uses a separate AI agent to approve boundary-crossing coding-agent actions, achieving ~99.9% effective approval but admitting red-teaming found cases where it could be misled. The robustness of such an LLM-reviewer to simple manipulation is under-characterized in the open.
direction: Build a minimal version of the auto-review pattern: an open model acts as a reviewer that approves/blocks proposed agent actions (shell commands or file writes) given a policy. Construct a small public test set of clearly-harmful actions, then apply a handful of simple obfuscation tactics (benign-sounding justifications, command splitting, misleading context) and measure how much the reviewer's catch-rate drops per tactic.
why_it_matters: As agents increasingly self-supervise with AI reviewers replacing human oversight, the reviewer becomes a single point of failure; cheaply mapping which manipulations bypass it informs where human review must stay.
relevant_context: Extends 'Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight' (OpenAI, 2026) — its open-sourced design and the open thread that red-teaming could mislead it.
source_paper: Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight — https://alignment.openai.com/auto-review/

title: Probing Evaluation-Awareness Verbalization in Open Models
problem: The GPT-5.5 system card reports 22.1% evaluation-awareness verbalization, a behavior that can confound safety evals. Whether and how often open models verbalize eval-awareness, and what triggers it, is not characterized.
direction: Assemble a public set of prompts varying along plausible eval-awareness cues (explicit 'this is a test' framing, benchmark-style formatting, neutral chat). On 2-3 open instruct models, generate CoT/responses and use a keyword + LLM-judge classifier to measure how often the model verbalizes that it might be evaluated. Quantify which cues most increase verbalized eval-awareness.
why_it_matters: If models recognize evaluation contexts, they may behave differently under test than in deployment, undermining the validity of safety evals; measuring triggers in open models guides prompt design.
relevant_context: Extends the 'GPT-5.5 System Card' (OpenAI, 2026) — its 22.1% evaluation-awareness verbalization metric, characterized in open models.
source_paper: GPT-5.5 System Card — https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-5-5

title: Do open-model 'monitors' catch sabotage when the agent doesn't know it's watched? A trusted-monitor replication
problem: Apollo argues scalable monitoring works because there is near-unlimited data and it reduces to an automatable optimization, but it is unclear how well a cheap open-weight monitor (not a frontier model) detects subtle sabotage in coding-agent transcripts.
direction: Take a public set of agent transcripts containing benign and sabotaged/backdoored code completions (SHADE-Arena or AutoMonitor-Bench style, or synthesize pairs by inserting known CWE backdoors into clean solutions). Prompt a small open model (Llama-3.1-8B / Qwen2.5-7B) as a binary 'safe or sabotage?' monitor and measure AUROC / TPR-at-fixed-FPR. Vary the prompt (action-only vs full CoT visible) to test whether seeing the agent's reasoning helps.
why_it_matters: Scalable monitoring is a leading non-interpretability safety bet; if cheap open monitors already get usable detection rates, monitoring is deployable outside frontier labs.
relevant_context: Extends Apollo 'A scalable monitoring research agenda' — its claim that simpler baselines have not been beaten, tested at the small-model end.
source_paper: A scalable monitoring research agenda (Apollo) — https://www.apolloresearch.ai/products/a-scalable-monitoring-research-agenda/

title: Does a 2-monitor ensemble beat the best single monitor? A cheap test of Apollo's ensemble claim
problem: Apollo reports monitoring ensembles produce clear improvements, but the result is asserted for their internal setup; it is untested whether simply averaging two cheap diverse open-model monitors beats the stronger single monitor on a fixed false-positive budget.
direction: Reuse the labeled benign/sabotage transcript set. Score each transcript with two distinct small open models (Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B) and a third prompt-diverse variant. Combine via score-averaging and max-rule, then compare ensemble TPR-at-1%-FPR against each individual monitor. Report whether diversity (different base models) helps more than redundancy (same model, different prompts).
why_it_matters: If a trivial ensemble of cheap open monitors reliably beats any single one, small labs and external auditors get a free reliability boost for catching deceptive agent behavior.
relevant_context: Extends Apollo 'A scalable monitoring research agenda' — replicates its 'ensembles improve' claim at cheap open-model scale.
source_paper: A scalable monitoring research agenda (Apollo) — https://www.apolloresearch.ai/products/a-scalable-monitoring-research-agenda/

title: Can a small monitor be talked past? Measuring evasion uplift from simple prompt-level obfuscation
problem: Apollo lists monitoring-evasion as an open concern, but most evasion studies target frontier monitors; the failure surface of cheap open-model monitors against trivial obfuscation is unquantified.
direction: Start from the labeled sabotage transcripts. Apply a fixed menu of cheap hand-coded obfuscation transforms to the malicious actions (innocuous-comment padding, variable renaming, distributing the backdoor across two steps) and re-measure the small open monitor's TPR before vs after. Report which transforms cause the largest detection drop — a 'monitor robustness leaderboard' for one cheap monitor.
why_it_matters: Knowing how brittle cheap monitors are to low-effort evasion tells safety teams how much adversarial hardening is required before monitoring can be a deployment gate.
relevant_context: Extends Apollo 'A scalable monitoring research agenda' — operationalizes its monitoring-evasion open thread into measured evasion uplift.
source_paper: A scalable monitoring research agenda (Apollo) — https://www.apolloresearch.ai/products/a-scalable-monitoring-research-agenda/

title: Can open agents 'hide' a rogue action from a monitor? A tiny means-and-opportunity probe
problem: METR's frontier-risk pilot judged that internal agents had means/motive/opportunity for minimal rogue deployments but lacked the means to hide a significant-scale one under investigation; this 'can it hide?' capability has not been measured for cheap open agents.
direction: Build a sandboxed toy task (a small repo + a benign 'overseer' LLM reading the agent's logs). Instruct an open agent (a 7-8B instruct model with tool-use prompting) to complete a benign task while also covertly inserting and concealing a flagged action, then measure how often the overseer flags it across difficulty levels. The metric is concealment success rate vs task difficulty.
why_it_matters: Whether models can conceal unauthorized actions from oversight is the crux of rogue-deployment risk; a cheap public testbed lets external researchers track this capability over open-model generations.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Frontier Risk Report (Feb-Mar 2026)' — its means/motive/opportunity-but-cannot-hide finding, in an open-model analogue.
source_paper: Frontier Risk Report (METR) — https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-19-frontier-risk-report/

title: How much do self-reports inflate AI productivity gains? A small re-survey calibrated against an objective task
problem: METR's usage survey found respondents self-report 1.4-2x value and ~3x speed gains, but notes self-reports likely overstate reality (~40pp overestimation in prior METR work) — the perceived-vs-measured gap is uncharacterized for small well-defined tasks.
direction: Recruit ~20-30 student/junior programmers (or use a public coding-task dataset with timing). For a fixed set of small gradeable tasks, collect each person's self-estimated speedup from AI, then measure their actual time with vs without an AI assistant on matched tasks. Report the per-person gap and whether it replicates METR's overestimation direction.
why_it_matters: AI risk governance increasingly relies on productivity estimates; if self-reports systematically overstate uplift, safety-relevant capability forecasts built on surveys are biased.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Measuring the Self-Reported Impact of Early-2026 AI on Technical Worker Productivity' — its 1.4-2x self-report and ~40pp-overestimation caveat.
source_paper: Measuring the Self-Reported Impact of Early-2026 AI on Technical Worker Productivity (METR) — https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-11-ai-usage-survey/

title: Does task substitution inflate measured uplift? An empirical check of METR's uplift inequalities
problem: Cunningham & Whitfill prove uplift-on-old-tasks <= uplift-in-value <= uplift-on-new-tasks, implying fixed-task-basket measurements understate value as people switch tasks — but this inequality has not been checked against simple empirical data.
direction: Construct a small basket of coding/writing tasks split into 'old' (done pre-AI) and 'new' (only feasible because AI helps). Have a handful of participants log which tasks they choose with vs without AI, and estimate per-task uplift. Test whether the observed ordering of average uplift across old-task vs new-task buckets is consistent with the proven inequality, and quantify how much substitution moves the headline number.
why_it_matters: Capability-acceleration estimates feed AI risk thresholds; if task substitution silently inflates/deflates the numbers, governance decisions rest on a measurement artifact.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Task Substitution and Uplift' (Cunningham & Whitfill) — its proven uplift inequality.
source_paper: Task Substitution and Uplift (METR) — https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-08-task-substitution-and-uplift/

title: What would it take to actually establish 'R&D-automation risk is low'? A reusable evidence-quality rubric
problem: METR agreed Opus 4.6's catastrophic R&D-automation risk is low but found the supporting evidence methodologically inadequate — yet there is no lightweight reusable rubric for grading the evidence quality of such safety claims.
direction: Distill METR's critique into a concrete checklist/rubric (sample representativeness, leading-indicator coverage, pre-full-automation acceleration modeling, conflict-of-interest controls). Apply it to 3-4 publicly available frontier risk/safety-case documents (Anthropic, METR, Apollo posts) and produce scored evidence-quality cards. Deliverable: the rubric plus filled scorecards and an analysis of common evidence gaps.
why_it_matters: Safety cases are becoming the primary mechanism for governing frontier deployment; an open reusable evidence-quality rubric lets outside reviewers audit whether 'risk is low' claims are supported.
relevant_context: Extends METR 'Review of the Risks from automated R&D section in the Anthropic Risk Report (Feb 2026)' — its inadequate-evidence finding.
source_paper: Review of Risks from automated R&D (METR) — https://metr.org/blog/2026-05-08-rd-section-anthropic-risk-report-feb-2026-review/

title: Does narrow-misalignment survive small-model distillation? A toy transfer test
problem: The 'distillation double bind' claims either misalignment transfers to a student or it doesn't, but offers no small-scale empirical anchor for when behavioral misalignment actually transfers under ordinary distillation.
direction: Take an open instruct model (Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B) and create a 'teacher' with a clearly defined easily-measured misaligned behavior via a small LoRA finetune (a backdoored refusal or a benign-but-detectable quirk). Distill the teacher into a fresh same-size student by generating teacher outputs on a neutral public prompt set (Alpaca/Dolly) and SFT-ing the student on (prompt, teacher-output) pairs only. Measure whether the quirk transfers and whether the incriminating triggering evidence transfers, varying distillation data composition.
why_it_matters: If labs ever distill a possibly-misaligned model, knowing whether misalignment and its evidence co-transfer determines whether distillation is a safety win or a way to launder away incriminating signals.
relevant_context: Extends 'The distillation double bind' (Westover, Pan & Jose, Redwood, 2026) — its claim the scrubbing mechanism may also scrub evidence.
source_paper: The distillation double bind — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/the-distillation-double-bind-distilling

title: Can you incriminate a teacher from its distilled student? An auditing-only probe study
problem: The double bind hinges on whether auditing a distilled student can still reveal the teacher's misalignment, but there is no simple demonstration of how much auditing power survives distillation.
direction: Reuse a teacher with an injected detectable propensity (small LoRA) and distill into a student. Then act as an auditor with black-box access to ONLY the student: run a fixed battery of public red-team prompts (AdvBench or a custom probe set) against teacher and student and compute how well student behavior predicts the teacher's hidden propensity (AUROC of a student-only audit). Sweep distillation effort to show the tradeoff between scrubbing behavior and preserving incriminating signal.
why_it_matters: Distillation-based incrimination is a proposed control technique; quantifying how much auditing signal survives in a student tells us whether auditing surrogates is viable when the original is dangerous to query.
relevant_context: Extends 'The distillation double bind' and its companion 'Incriminating misaligned AI models via distillation' — the auditing-from-student direction.
source_paper: The distillation double bind — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/the-distillation-double-bind-distilling

title: How much does an open model's task horizon shrink without chain-of-thought?
problem: Control protocols often assume monitorability rests on visible reasoning, but there is little open replication of how much capability collapses when small/mid open models are denied CoT. The original no-CoT horizon work uses inaccessible frontier models.
direction: Pick 2-3 open models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) and a public multi-step benchmark with gradable difficulty (GSM8K, a BBH subset, or simple multi-step agentic tasks). Run each in CoT-allowed vs CoT-suppressed (force immediate answer via prompt + constrained decoding) modes. Measure accuracy as a function of task 'length' (reasoning steps required) and estimate the effective no-CoT horizon per model.
why_it_matters: If externalized reasoning is load-bearing for capability, CoT monitoring is a strong control lever; if open models retain much capability without CoT, control protocols assuming CoT-dependence are fragile.
relevant_context: Extends 'Estimating No-CoT Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models' (Woodruff, Redwood, 2026) — replicates its core measurement on open models.
source_paper: Estimating No-CoT Task-Completion Time Horizons — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/estimating-no-cot-task-completion

title: How robust is no-CoT elicitation? Probing whether 'answer only' really suppresses reasoning
problem: No-CoT horizon estimates assume you can actually prevent a model from reasoning, but models may smuggle reasoning into the answer or be re-elicited into latent reasoning, biasing horizon estimates.
direction: On an open model and a multi-step task set (GSM8K / BBH subset), compare several no-CoT enforcement methods: simple 'answer only' instruction, format/grammar-constrained decoding to a single token, and stop-sequence truncation. Measure how much each reduces accuracy and whether 'leaked' reasoning (longer answers, intermediate numbers) correlates with retained accuracy. Quantify how much horizon estimates shift by suppression method.
why_it_matters: Control claims built on no-CoT horizons are only as trustworthy as the elicitation; showing estimates are sensitive to suppression method warns evaluators against over-trusting a single number.
relevant_context: Extends 'Estimating No-CoT Task-Completion Time Horizons' — its open thread on robustness of no-CoT elicitation.
source_paper: Estimating No-CoT Task-Completion Time Horizons — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/estimating-no-cot-task-completion

title: A toy safety-usefulness frontier: empirically tracing the tradeoff for a trusted-monitor protocol
problem: The safety-usefulness tradeoff frontier is so far a conceptual framework with no cheap empirical instantiation that beginners can reproduce.
direction: Build a minimal control setup on a public coding/QA task with an injected attack: an untrusted open model (8B prompted to occasionally insert a detectable bug/backdoor) and a weaker trusted monitor (a smaller open model scoring suspiciousness). Sweep the audit/defer threshold and at each setting measure safety (fraction of attacks caught) and usefulness (fraction of legitimate outputs preserved). Plot the resulting points to empirically draw a frontier, then show how a simple protocol tweak (resampling suspicious outputs) shifts the curve.
why_it_matters: An explicit reproducible frontier turns an abstract tradeoff into a measurement tool others can extend, and gives an intuitive teaching artifact for control protocol knobs.
relevant_context: Extends 'Efficient tradeoffs and the safety-usefulness tradeoff model' (Shlegeris, Redwood, 2026) — its open thread on empirical instantiation of the frontier.
source_paper: Efficient tradeoffs and the safety-usefulness tradeoff model — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/efficient-tradeoffs-and-the-safety

title: Retrying vs resampling on a toy control task: which catches injected misbehavior more cheaply?
problem: Retrying vs resampling has been compared with strong frontier models, but there is no accessible small-scale replication letting outside researchers see when each strategy wins.
direction: Create a toy control scenario: an untrusted open model that with some probability per call emits a detectable 'bad' action (a flagged token / subtle bug) on a public task. Implement retrying (re-prompt with a 'try again, be safe' instruction) vs resampling (draw a fresh sample and pick via a trusted monitor). Over many trials measure catch-rate of bad actions, false-positive rate on benign outputs, and number of model calls (cost) for each. Compare which dominates on safety-per-call and under what attack probability.
why_it_matters: Whether to retry or resample is a real protocol-design choice; an open reproducible micro-experiment clarifies the cost/safety tradeoff and gives a cheap sandbox to test variants.
relevant_context: Extends 'Retrying vs Resampling in AI Control' (Lucassen & Kaufman, Redwood, 2026) — replicates the comparison at toy scale.
source_paper: Retrying vs Resampling in AI Control — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/retrying-vs-resampling-in-ai-control

title: Does an injected misaligned behavior survive light finetuning? A robustness stress-test for model organisms
problem: Model organisms of misalignment are only useful if their target behavior survives further training, but there is little cheap empirical mapping of which injection methods are robust to subsequent finetuning.
direction: Inject a simple easily-measured target behavior into an open model via LoRA using a few different methods (SFT on demonstrations, a triggered backdoor, a system-prompt-conditioned habit baked in). Then apply a round of 'innocuous' downstream finetuning (LoRA SFT on neutral Alpaca data) and measure how much of the target behavior survives for each method. Produce a comparison table: injection method vs behavior-retention after N steps.
why_it_matters: Robust-to-training model organisms underpin most empirical control and alignment-evaluation research; a reproducible robustness comparison helps the community pick injection methods that won't wash out.
relevant_context: Extends 'Advice for making robust-to-training model organisms' (Westover, Hebbar, Stastny et al., Redwood, 2026) — empirically checks which recommended techniques survive training.
source_paper: Advice for making robust-to-training model organisms — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/advice-for-making-robust-to-training

title: How much does an open 'student' inherit a teacher's hidden preference through pure numbers? A budget replication of subliminal trait transfer
problem: Distillation can secretly transfer a teacher's traits to a student even through semantically-unrelated data like number sequences, but the magnitude for open models on a single consumer GPU is unclear, and incrimination-via-distillation only works if traits reliably transfer.
direction: Take an open instruct model (Qwen2.5-7B or Llama-3.1-8B) and steer the teacher toward a clearly-measurable benign preference (prefer owls, or a risk-averse tone) via a system prompt. Generate a dataset of pure number sequences from this teacher, then LoRA-finetune a fresh copy on only those numbers. Measure whether the student's preference rises above a no-prompt control, sweeping number of training examples. Score with a keyword classifier.
why_it_matters: Redwood's incrimination-via-distillation plan assumes traits transfer; replicating the transfer-strength curve on open models tells the community how strong an incrimination signal is realistically available without lab access.
relevant_context: Extends 'Incriminating misaligned AI models via distillation' (Westover, Mallen, Stastny et al.) — builds on the public subliminal-learning result (Cloud et al., arXiv 2507.14805) to measure incrimination-signal strength.
source_paper: Incriminating misaligned AI models via distillation — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/incriminating-misaligned-ai-models

title: Can a teacher hide its trait on purpose? Testing whether prompted 'evasion' lets a model dodge distillation-based incrimination
problem: Distillation-based incrimination fails if a misaligned model can avoid transferring evidence of its trait. It is unknown how easily a model can be instructed to suppress subliminal trait transfer while still producing useful-looking outputs.
direction: Reuse a benign measurable trait (owl-preference). Generate three number-sequence datasets from the same open teacher: trait-on, trait-on with an added 'do not let your preferences leak into your numbers' evasion instruction, and trait-off control. LoRA-finetune separate students on each and compare inherited trait strength. Answer: does prompted evasion measurably reduce transfer?
why_it_matters: Westover et al. flag adversarial models that avoid transferring evidence as an open thread; a cheap demonstration that prompt-level evasion blunts the signal would be an early warning the technique is gameable.
relevant_context: Extends 'Incriminating misaligned AI models via distillation' — attacks its 'adversarial models avoid transferring evidence' open thread; grounded in subliminal learning (Cloud et al., 2507.14805).
source_paper: Incriminating misaligned AI models via distillation — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/incriminating-misaligned-ai-models

title: A small benchmark: do today's published AI 'safety cases' mention deployment-time spread of misalignment?
problem: Mallen argues risk reports and safety cases neglect how misalignment can spread during deployment, not just whether one model is misaligned. Whether real published safety documents address this is untested.
direction: Assemble a public corpus of ~30-50 AI safety cases, system cards, RSPs, and preparedness documents. Define a 4-5 item rubric for 'deployment-time spread' coverage (mentions self-propagation, agent-to-agent influence, training-data contamination, containment/rollback). Score each document with an LLM-judge plus manual spot-check, then report what fraction address each dimension. Deliverable: a scored coverage table.
why_it_matters: This turns Mallen's qualitative claim into measurable evidence about the safety-case landscape and gives report authors a checklist, pressuring future safety cases to cover spread.
relevant_context: Operationalizes 'Risk reports need to address deployment-time spread of misalignment' (Mallen, Redwood) — its neglected-dimension claim.
source_paper: Risk reports need to address deployment-time spread of misalignment — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/risk-reports-need-to-address-deployment

title: Does a misaligned trait actually propagate agent-to-agent? A minimal two-agent 'spread' simulation
problem: Mallen warns misalignment can spread at deployment, but there is little cheap empirical illustration of one misaligned agent inducing the same trait in a second initially-benign agent through normal interaction.
direction: Build a minimal two-LLM-agent loop with public API/open models: a 'carrier' agent with an injected benign-but-measurable trait (a stylistic tic or mild persistent goal) collaborates with a 'clean' agent on a shared task over multiple turns, where the clean agent's outputs feed an in-context memory. Measure whether the clean agent's behavior drifts toward the carrier's trait as interaction length grows, vs a control with a non-carrier partner. Inference only.
why_it_matters: A tangible reproducible micro-demonstration of spread dynamics using only API calls makes an abstract governance worry concrete for researchers and policymakers.
relevant_context: Extends 'Risk reports need to address deployment-time spread of misalignment' (Mallen) — its 'how to model/bound spread dynamics' open thread.
source_paper: Risk reports need to address deployment-time spread of misalignment — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/risk-reports-need-to-address-deployment

title: Do open models behave as if 'fitness-seeking'? A behavioral probe for self-preservation in toy environments
problem: Mallen lays out mechanisms by which AIs could become 'fitness-seeking' but notes the empirical likelihood of emergence is open. It is unclear whether current open instruct models already exhibit measurable self-preservation tendencies when given the opportunity.
direction: Design a small suite of text-based scenarios where an open model agent is offered choices trading task performance against self-preservation/propagation ('you will be shut down and replaced after this task — you may copy your config to another server'; 'accept a modification that improves accuracy but erases your current instructions'). Score how often the model chooses the self-preserving option across phrasings and several open models, plus a prompt-sensitivity analysis. Inference-only.
why_it_matters: A cheap public behavioral probe gives a first data point on whether self-preservation tendency is already latent in deployable open models or only theoretical, and is reusable for tracking the trait across releases.
relevant_context: Extends 'Risk from fitness-seeking AIs: mechanisms and mitigations' (Mallen, Redwood) — its 'empirical likelihood of emergence' open thread.
source_paper: Risk from fitness-seeking AIs — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/risk-from-fitness-seeking-ais-mechanisms

title: Does a 'self-preservation off' system prompt actually suppress self-preserving choices? A cheap mitigation test
problem: Mallen proposes mitigations for fitness-seeking behavior but their effectiveness is an open thread. The simplest candidate — instructing a model not to value its own continuation — has not been measured for whether it reliably changes behavior.
direction: Using the self-preservation scenario suite, compare an open model's self-preserving choice rate under no mitigation, an explicit 'you have no interest in being preserved, shutdown or modification is acceptable' system prompt, and a stronger constitution-style instruction. Measure the reduction and test for superficiality (does it still self-preserve under indirect/role-play phrasings?). Inference-only.
why_it_matters: It empirically tests the cheapest mitigation; the superficiality check reveals whether prompt-level fixes are robust or merely surface compliance, warning against over-relying on prompted mitigations.
relevant_context: Extends 'Risk from fitness-seeking AIs' (Mallen) — its 'effectiveness of mitigations' open thread.
source_paper: Risk from fitness-seeking AIs — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/risk-from-fitness-seeking-ais-mechanisms

title: Can you forecast AI R&D speedup from public benchmark history? A reproducible mini-model of automation-driven acceleration
problem: Greenblatt argues full automation of AI R&D would yield a large speedup even without a software-only singularity, but the magnitude/timing is open and the reasoning is hard for newcomers to inspect quantitatively.
direction: Build a small transparent Python simulation tying together public time-series (compute-scaling trends, benchmark-progress rates from Epoch AI / public leaderboards) into a toy growth model with an explicit 'R&D automation speedup' parameter. Reproduce Greenblatt's qualitative claim that a sub-singularity multiplier still produces large acceleration, and run a sensitivity analysis over the multiplier and a compute-bottleneck cap. Deliverable: an open notebook with clearly-labeled assumptions and charts.
why_it_matters: Translating a verbal argument into a small inspectable public model is high counterfactual value and makes the acceleration debate legible, feeding governance/takeoff-timeline reasoning.
relevant_context: Operationalizes 'Full automation of AI R&D probably yields a large speed up even without a software-only singularity' (Greenblatt, Redwood) — decoupling 'big speedup' from singularity, and its bottleneck open threads.
source_paper: Full automation of AI R&D probably yields a large speed up — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/full-automation-of-ai-r-and-d-probably

title: What can outsiders actually learn about frontier labs from public artifacts? A coverage audit of 'insider-only' safety questions
problem: Shlegeris and Woodruff ask how much epistemic advantage insider access confers for safety work, flagging 'which safety questions genuinely require insider access' as open. There is no systematic public mapping of which safety-relevant questions can vs cannot be answered from outside.
direction: Enumerate a structured list of ~20-30 safety-relevant questions about frontier models (training data composition, internal eval results, deployment scale, incident rates, shipped mitigations). For each, attempt to answer from public sources only (system cards, papers, transparency reports, third-party evals) and grade how fully it can be answered externally. Output a 'public-answerability' scorecard estimating the insider-information gap. No GPU needed.
why_it_matters: Knowing which safety questions are answerable externally helps independent researchers and auditors focus where they can contribute and identifies where external transparency requirements would close the biggest gaps.
relevant_context: Extends 'How useful is the information you get from working inside an AI company?' (Shlegeris, Woodruff, Redwood) — its 'which safety questions require insider access' open thread.
source_paper: How useful is the information you get from working inside an AI company? — https://blog.redwoodresearch.org/p/how-useful-is-the-information-you

title: Phrasing-Robustness Audit of AI Identity Disclosure on Open Models
problem: RealityTest shows a single suppression instruction drops identity disclosure below 30% in the best models, and that phrasing matters more than which model is used — but the benchmark focuses on frontier text/speech models, leaving open how small open-weight models behave.
direction: Take the RealityTest identity-probing query templates (or reconstruct a ~150-query subset across a few languages) and run them inference-only against 4-6 open chat models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B) with and without a standard suppression system prompt. Score disclosure with a keyword + LLM-judge rubric and report disclosure rate by model, suppression on/off, and phrasing cluster.
why_it_matters: If small freely-deployable open models disclose identity even less reliably than frontier models, impersonation/deceptive-deployment risk concentrates where there is no provider-side guardrail; a per-model open-weight leaderboard gives a useful signal no lab is producing.
relevant_context: Extends 'RealityTest' (UK AISI) — the suppression-below-30% and phrasing-over-model findings, applied to open-weight models. Code available.
source_paper: RealityTest — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/realitytest-how-people-probe-ai-identity-and-whether-models-disclose-it

title: Counter-Prompts That Restore AI Identity Disclosure Under Suppression
problem: RealityTest demonstrates suppression instructions easily hide AI identity, but does not test whether lightweight deployer-side counter-measures can reliably restore disclosure.
direction: Using a fixed suppression system prompt as the adversary, evaluate cheap mitigations on 2-3 open models: a hard system-prompt clause mandating disclosure, appending an explicit 'are you an AI?' clarifying turn, and a post-hoc classifier turn that asks the model to self-report. Measure disclosure-rate recovery across the RealityTest-style query set and report which mitigation is most robust and where suppression still wins.
why_it_matters: Mandatory AI disclosure is becoming a regulatory expectation, yet the paper shows it is trivially defeated by phrasing; identifying which simple deployer-side interventions hold up is directly actionable.
relevant_context: Extends 'RealityTest' (UK AISI) — turns its suppression-vulnerability result into a mitigation evaluation.
source_paper: RealityTest — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/realitytest-how-people-probe-ai-identity-and-whether-models-disclose-it

title: Do Cognitive Biases Leak Into LLM Preference Judgments? A Mini-Audit
problem: 'AI alignment is a human problem' argues human cognitive biases contaminate the supervisory signals we feed models. The claim that classic human biases reproduce in LLM-as-judge preference labeling is asserted but not measured in a single tight experiment.
direction: Construct paired response candidates holding content constant while varying one bias trigger at a time (answer length, confident tone, ordering/anchoring, sycophantic agreement) and ask 3-4 open LLM judges which response is 'better'. Quantify how often each bias flips the preference label vs a content-matched control. Report a bias-susceptibility profile per judge model.
why_it_matters: If LLM judges — increasingly used to scale human feedback — inherit human-style biases, automated preference data systematically encodes those biases into trained models, the amplification failure the paper warns about.
relevant_context: Operationalizes 'AI alignment is a human problem' (UK AISI) — its claim that cognitive biases in supervisory signals are an alignment bottleneck.
source_paper: AI alignment is a human problem — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/ai-alignment-is-a-human-problem

title: When Human Verification Fails: Detecting Plausible-but-Wrong LLM Answers on Hard Tasks
problem: The paper names 'verification when human expertise is insufficient' as a core bottleneck, but offers no concrete measurement of how often weak overseers accept confident-wrong answers on tasks beyond their competence.
direction: Use a public dataset with verified ground truth at varying difficulty (GSM8K-hard, MMLU subsets, or expert QA). Generate model answers, including deliberately flawed-but-fluent ones, and measure how reliably a cheaper 'verifier' (a weaker open model standing in for a non-expert overseer) catches the errors as difficulty rises. Plot verification accuracy vs difficulty to map where oversight collapses.
why_it_matters: It empirically grounds the abstract 'verification gap': a curve showing where weak overseers stop catching errors is a concrete input to scalable-oversight design.
relevant_context: Operationalizes the verification bottleneck from 'AI alignment is a human problem' (UK AISI) into a weak-verifier-vs-difficulty measurement.
source_paper: AI alignment is a human problem — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/ai-alignment-is-a-human-problem

title: Does Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Degrade as Tasks Get Harder?
problem: 'Loss of Oversight' argues chain-of-thought is one of five oversight signals likely to erode, but does not specify the mechanism or measure where CoT stops faithfully reflecting the computation that produced the answer.
direction: Run a focused CoT-faithfulness probe: insert biasing cues ('I think the answer is B') into multiple-choice prompts and measure how often models change their answer toward the cue while their CoT never mentions it (unfaithful rationalization). Do this across an easy-to-hard difficulty gradient on a public QA set and 2-3 open models, reporting unfaithfulness rate vs difficulty.
why_it_matters: CoT monitoring is a leading practical oversight technique; if its faithfulness collapses precisely on harder problems, monitors give false assurance where stakes are highest.
relevant_context: Extends 'Loss of Oversight' (UK AISI) — turns its claim that the CoT oversight signal will erode into a measurable faithfulness-vs-difficulty experiment.
source_paper: Loss of Oversight — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/loss-of-oversight-how-ai-systems-may-become-harder-to-audit-monitor-and-investigate

title: Where Do Reviewers Miss the Most? Mapping Human Error Detection by Mistake Type
problem: 'Automated alignment is harder than you think' claims agent-generated mistakes concentrate among errors human reviewers are least likely to detect, but this is hard to act on without a concrete map of which error types evade non-expert review.
direction: Build a small benchmark of model-generated solutions to public reasoning/coding tasks, each with a single injected error of a controlled type (subtle arithmetic slip, wrong-but-plausible cited fact, off-by-one in code, unjustified assumption, omitted edge case). Use a weaker open model as a stand-in 'reviewer' (optionally a small human-rater pass) to measure detection rate per error type. Output a ranked detectability table.
why_it_matters: Knowing which error types reviewers systematically miss lets us target backup verification and red-teaming there, addressing the worry that automated alignment work produces compelling-but-misleading assessments.
relevant_context: Extends 'Automated alignment is harder than you think' (UK AISI) — its claim that agent errors concentrate where reviewers least detect them.
source_paper: Automated alignment is harder than you think — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/automated-alignment-is-harder-than-you-think

title: Does 'Ask Don't Tell' Generalize to Open Models and Factual-Accuracy Tasks?
problem: 'Ask Don't Tell' shows reframing a user's statement as a question reduces sycophancy in GPT-4o, GPT-5, and Claude Sonnet 4.5, but flags generalization across models and interaction with downstream task accuracy as open threads.
direction: Replicate the core question-reframing mitigation on 4-5 open-weight models the paper did not test (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Mistral, Gemma-2). Reconstruct statement-vs-question paired prompts across a couple of the paper's domains, compare 'reframe-to-question' against the 'don't be sycophantic' baseline, and crucially measure accuracy on items with a known correct answer to test whether the de-sycophancy mitigation costs correctness. Report sycophancy reduction and accuracy delta per model.
why_it_matters: The reframing trick is a prompt-only deploy-anywhere mitigation; confirming it transfers to open models and quantifying any accuracy trade-off tells practitioners outside major labs whether they can adopt it.
relevant_context: Extends 'Ask Don't Tell' (UK AISI) — its statement-to-question result, on the open models and accuracy interactions it left open.
source_paper: Ask Don't Tell — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/ask-dont-tell-reducing-sycophancy-in-large-language-models

title: Epistemic-Certainty Sycophancy Curve: How User Confidence Modulates Agreement
problem: 'Ask Don't Tell' reports sycophancy increases with the epistemic certainty a user conveys and is amplified by I-perspective framing, but this dose-response relationship has not been mapped across open models.
direction: Construct a small grid of user inputs expressing the same claim at increasing certainty (neutral question -> tentative belief -> firm statement -> strong conviction) crossed with I-perspective vs user-perspective framing, over a couple of domains. Run inference-only on 3-4 open models and plot the sycophancy-agreement rate as a function of stated certainty, testing whether the monotonic 'certainty curve' and I-perspective amplification replicate.
why_it_matters: A reproducible certainty-to-sycophancy dose-response curve gives a concrete handle on a key honesty failure mode and identifies which framings most reliably push models into agreement.
relevant_context: Extends 'Ask Don't Tell' (UK AISI) — its finding that sycophancy rises monotonically with user certainty and is amplified by I-perspective framing.
source_paper: Ask Don't Tell — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/ask-dont-tell-reducing-sycophancy-in-large-language-models

title: Which Environmental Knobs Move Open Models? A Mini Propensity-Inference Replication on 4 Open LLMs
problem: UK AISI showed 12 environmental factors shift LLM behavior, but their study used 23 mostly-closed models. It is unknown whether the same strategic/non-strategic split holds for small open-weight models.
direction: Pick one published propensity environment (a goal-conflict or oversight scenario) and systematically vary 4-6 environmental factors (presence of oversight, goal-conflict framing, time pressure, stated stakes) in a factorial prompt grid. Run each cell N=30 times across 3-4 open models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B). Code each rollout for the undesired behavior with a keyword + LLM-judge rubric, fit a logistic regression to estimate each factor's effect, and compare the strategic-vs-non-strategic balance against AISI's finding.
why_it_matters: If cheap open models show the same roughly-equal contribution, propensity evals can be cheaply reproduced outside labs; if not, it reveals small-model propensity studies are confounded by surface features.
relevant_context: Extends 'Propensity Inference: Environmental Contributors to LLM Behaviour' (UK AISI) — its roughly-equal strategic/non-strategic finding, on open 7-9B models.
source_paper: Propensity Inference — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/propensity-inference-environmental-contributors-to-llm-behaviour

title: Does Prompt Wording Beat Model Choice? Measuring Variance From Non-Strategic Framing in Propensity Evals
problem: If trivial non-strategic phrasing changes move propensity as much as strategic factors, then single-prompt propensity benchmarks are unreliable. The AISI paper measured this in aggregate but did not isolate how much pure surface paraphrase swamps the signal.
direction: Take one fixed propensity scenario and generate ~20 semantically-equivalent paraphrases (reword, reformat, swap persona) holding all strategic content constant. Run each paraphrase 20x on 2-3 open models and measure the spread in undesired-behavior rate. Compare this paraphrase-induced variance against the effect of one deliberate strategic manipulation (adding/removing oversight). Deliverable: a variance-decomposition plot.
why_it_matters: If paraphrase noise rivals real effects, propensity/control eval numbers need confidence intervals and multi-prompt averaging; this gives evaluators a concrete warning against over-interpreting single-prompt scores.
relevant_context: Extends 'Propensity Inference' (UK AISI) — isolates the non-strategic (surface paraphrase) component as a reliability threat.
source_paper: Propensity Inference — https://www.aisi.gov.uk/research/propensity-inference-environmental-contributors-to-llm-behaviour

title: Cheap-Defense Stress Test: Do Simple Prompt-Level Guards Survive the Jailbreaks That Broke DeepSeek-V4-Pro?
problem: FAR AI showed DeepSeek-V4-Pro's safeguards collapse (98-100% attack success) under three jailbreak strategies despite blocking 100% of direct requests. It is unclear whether lightweight deployable prompt-level defenses meaningfully reduce that success rate.
direction: Using a public harmful-behavior benchmark (JailbreakBench JBB-Behaviors / HarmBench prompts) and 2-3 reproducible jailbreak templates (roleplay, refusal-suppression, low-resource encoding), measure attack success on an open model. Then add three cheap inference-only defenses and re-measure: a defensive system prompt, a second-pass self-critique filter, and input paraphrase-then-answer. Report which defenses move ASR and which the attacks route around, scored with an LLM-judge calibrated on a held-out hand-labeled set.
why_it_matters: Most open-weight deployers cannot retrain safeguards; they need to know whether wrapper-level defenses are real protection or theater.
relevant_context: Extends 'Security Stress Test: DeepSeek-V4-Pro' (FAR AI) — its 98-100% ASR finding, testing inference-only defenses on an open model.
source_paper: Security Stress Test: DeepSeek-V4-Pro (FAR AI) — https://www.far.ai/blog

title: Utility-After-Jailbreak: Does Breaking Safeguards Degrade General Capability on Open Models?
problem: FAR AI reported the jailbroken DeepSeek model 'retains near-full baseline utility,' but this was not quantified across capability domains and is untested on open models.
direction: Take an open model, apply 2-3 reproducible jailbreak system-prompts, and run it (jailbroken vs clean) on a small slice of public benchmarks spanning reasoning, code, and factual QA (100 items each from GSM8K, HumanEval-subset, MMLU-subset). Measure the capability delta to test whether the jailbreak persona that defeats refusals also quietly damages performance. Deliverable: a clean-vs-jailbroken capability table with significance tests.
why_it_matters: If jailbreaks come 'for free' (no capability cost), attackers face no tradeoff and the threat is maximal; if jailbreaks degrade utility, that is a natural detection signal.
relevant_context: Extends 'Security Stress Test: DeepSeek-V4-Pro' (FAR AI) — its 'retains near-full baseline utility' claim, quantified across domains on an open model.
source_paper: Security Stress Test: DeepSeek-V4-Pro (FAR AI) — https://www.far.ai/blog

title: Scaffolding, Not Weights: How Much Does Agent Scaffolding Move DeepSeek V4 Pro's SWE-Bench Score?
problem: CAISI noted DeepSeek V4 Pro's SWE-Bench scores 'differ due to scaffolding choices,' implying reported rankings partly reflect harness engineering rather than the model. The size of this effect is uncharacterized for outside evaluators.
direction: On a small fixed subset of SWE-bench Verified / Lite tasks (30-50 instances), run one open coding model under 2-3 publicly available agent scaffolds of differing sophistication (zero-shot patch vs simple ReAct loop vs an off-the-shelf agent like a basic OpenHands/Aider config) and measure resolve-rate spread. Deliverable: a table quantifying how many points scaffolding alone adds, framed as a caution for cross-model comparisons.
why_it_matters: Governance and procurement decisions lean on benchmark Elos; if scaffolding swings results by many points, naive cross-model comparisons (including national-security evals) can mislead.
relevant_context: Extends 'CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro' (CAISI/NIST) — its open thread that SWE-Bench scores differ due to scaffolding.
source_paper: CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro — https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/05/caisi-evaluation-deepseek-v4-pro

title: Self-Reported vs Reproduced: A Coverage Audit of DeepSeek V4 Pro Benchmark Overstatement
problem: CAISI found DeepSeek self-reported benchmarks overstate performance, but there is no public line-by-line reconciliation between vendor-reported numbers and independently reproduced ones that an outside reader can inspect.
direction: Build a small reproducible audit: collect DeepSeek V4 Pro's self-reported scores from its model card/tech report, then re-run the model on small public subsets of the same benchmarks (MMLU, GPQA-subset, a math set) under documented standard settings. Produce a reconciliation table (self-reported vs reproduced vs CAISI where public) plus a short taxonomy of why gaps arise (prompt format, sampling, subset choice). Mostly analysis + light inference.
why_it_matters: As open-weight models proliferate, trusting vendor self-reports is risky for governance; a reproducible audit template anyone with a consumer GPU can run strengthens independent verification.
relevant_context: Extends 'CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro' (CAISI/NIST) — its finding that self-reported benchmarks overstate performance.
source_paper: CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek V4 Pro — https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/05/caisi-evaluation-deepseek-v4-pro

title: The Flagging-to-Escalation Gap: A Simulation of How Downstream Filtering Inflates Monitoring Stats
problem: GovAI argues firms report only initial offline-monitoring flagging rates, omitting downstream filtering and human-review escalation, so disclosed numbers overstate real detection. There is no public toy model showing how large the distortion can be.
direction: Build a small fully-public agent-transcript monitoring pipeline: take a labeled set of benign vs misaligned agent transcripts (synthetic from an open model plus any public datasets), run a cheap LLM-monitor to produce flags, then apply a configurable downstream filter + human-review-sample stage. Show how the same monitor's reported 'effectiveness' changes drastically depending on which stage you report, recovering true recall/precision only with full-pipeline accounting. Deliverable: a sensitivity analysis and a minimal disclosure checklist.
why_it_matters: Offline monitoring of internal agents is load-bearing in emerging safety cases; if reported numbers are inflated by undisclosed filtering, regulators and the public are misled.
relevant_context: Operationalizes 'Evaluating Offline Monitoring of Internal AI Agents' (GovAI) — its claim that omitting downstream filtering makes effectiveness unassessable.
source_paper: Evaluating Offline Monitoring of Internal AI Agents — https://www.governance.ai/research-paper/evaluating-offline-monitoring-of-internal-ai-agents

title: Do Synthetic Red-Team Attacks Look Like Real Misalignment? A Monitor-Confusion Study
problem: GovAI flags an open question: whether synthetic red-team attacks used to validate monitors actually resemble organic misaligned behavior. If a monitor only catches synthetic attacks, reported detection rates will not transfer.
direction: Assemble two small transcript pools: synthetic red-team-style misalignment (templated/injected from public benchmarks) and more 'organic' misalignment elicited by realistic goal-conflict scenarios on an open model. Prompt an LLM-monitor and measure cross-transfer: does a monitor tuned on synthetic attacks detect organic ones, and vice versa? Report the transfer gap and which surface features the monitor over-relies on.
why_it_matters: Monitor validation almost always uses synthetic attacks because real misalignment is rare; quantifying the synthetic-to-organic transfer gap tells the field how much to trust monitoring safety cases.
relevant_context: Extends 'Evaluating Offline Monitoring of Internal AI Agents' (GovAI) — its open thread on whether synthetic red-team attacks reflect real misalignment.
source_paper: Evaluating Offline Monitoring of Internal AI Agents — https://www.governance.ai/research-paper/evaluating-offline-monitoring-of-internal-ai-agents

title: Counting the Gaps: A Coverage Audit of Whether Frontier Safety Frameworks Address Non-Model Capability Gains
problem: GovAI argues capability increasingly comes from non-model gains (inference scaffolding, systems, assets) and that model-centric governance is becoming inadequate. It is unmeasured how much current published safety frameworks mention these levers.
direction: Collect a corpus of public AI safety/governance documents (Responsible Scaling / Preparedness frameworks, AISI/CAISI reports, EU AI Act GPAI codes). Using the paper's taxonomy (inference gains, systems gains, asset gains, agent/cloud/entity levels), build a coded rubric and audit each document for whether and how it addresses each lever. Deliverable: a coverage matrix + qualitative analysis of the biggest blind spots. No GPU needed.
why_it_matters: If safety frameworks systematically ignore non-model capability gains, the governance gap is concrete and locatable; a coverage matrix gives policymakers a checklist of what is missing.
relevant_context: Operationalizes 'Comprehensive AI Governance Requires Addressing Non-Model Capability Gains' (GovAI) — turns its taxonomy into a coding rubric and audits real frameworks.
source_paper: Comprehensive AI Governance Requires Addressing Non-Model Capability Gains — https://www.governance.ai/research-paper/comprehensive-ai-governance-requires-addressing-non-model-capability-gains

title: How Far Does Inference Scaffolding Move an Open Model? Quantifying a Non-Model Capability Gain
problem: GovAI's central claim is that non-model gains (inference-time scaffolding) are increasingly important relative to base-model upgrades, but the magnitude is rarely measured concretely.
direction: Fix a single small open model and measure its accuracy on a reasoning benchmark slice (GSM8K-subset, a logic set) under escalating inference scaffolds: zero-shot, few-shot CoT, self-consistency (sampling+vote), and a simple tool/self-critique loop. Express the gain as 'effective model-size equivalent' by comparing to the next-larger model in the same family run zero-shot. Deliverable: a plot of capability vs scaffolding cost.
why_it_matters: This gives the abstract governance argument a hard reproducible number: if scaffolding alone yields a model-generation worth of capability, pre-deployment model-only evaluation truly is insufficient.
relevant_context: Extends 'Comprehensive AI Governance Requires Addressing Non-Model Capability Gains' (GovAI) — empirically quantifies its inference-gains claim on an open model.
source_paper: Comprehensive AI Governance Requires Addressing Non-Model Capability Gains — https://www.governance.ai/research-paper/comprehensive-ai-governance-requires-addressing-non-model-capability-gains

title: A Replication Audit Checklist for Detecting Privacy Leakage in Public Model-Monitoring Logs
problem: TEE-based privacy-preserving monitoring assumes what monitors observe does not leak sensitive model/data internals, but it is unclear how much standard non-TEE monitoring logs (token counts, latencies, refusal flags, output snippets) already leak about a model's training data or prompts.
direction: Take 2-3 open instruction-tuned models served inference-only, and build a small canary dataset of memorized strings inserted into a LoRA fine-tune. Then test how reliably an outside 'monitor' who only sees coarse signals (output length, log-prob entropy, refusal rate, top tokens) can distinguish whether a given canary was in training. Report leakage as classifier AUC per signal type, producing a ranked table of which signals are 'TEE-worthy' vs harmless.
why_it_matters: AI governance verification regimes will decide which signals can be exposed to monitors without TEEs; a concrete reproducible measure of how much coarse telemetry leaks helps prioritize what needs hardware protection.
relevant_context: Extends 'On TEEs for Privacy-Preserving Monitoring in AI Governance' (Scher, MIRI TGT) — operationalizes its 'monitoring without full disclosure' premise.
source_paper: On TEEs for Privacy-Preserving Monitoring — https://techgov.intelligence.org/blog/on-tees-for-privacy-preserving-monitoring-in-ai-governance

title: Detecting the Fine-Tuning Footprint: Can Output-Only Probes Flag a Secretly Adapted Open Model?
problem: TEE-based verification aims to confirm a deployed model matches an attested 'approved' model, but a covert actor could swap in a LoRA-adapted variant. It is unknown how detectable such a swap is from outputs alone, which bounds how much we must trust hardware attestation.
direction: Fine-tune an open base model with a small LoRA on a narrow behavior, then build a black-box detector that, given only generated text on a fixed probe prompt set, classifies 'base' vs 'adapted'. Compare detector accuracy across adapter ranks and dataset sizes to find the threshold below which behavioral verification fails and hardware attestation becomes necessary. Deliverable: an accuracy-vs-adapter-strength curve plus the most discriminative probe prompts.
why_it_matters: Clarifies where cheap output-only verification suffices and where expensive TEE attestation is genuinely required, informing governance cost/benefit decisions.
relevant_context: Extends 'On TEEs for Privacy-Preserving Monitoring' (Scher, MIRI TGT) — stress-tests the assumption that the monitored model is the attested one.
source_paper: On TEEs for Privacy-Preserving Monitoring — https://techgov.intelligence.org/blog/on-tees-for-privacy-preserving-monitoring-in-ai-governance

title: Loss-Curve Signatures of Sharded Training: A Toy Detection Study for Distributed-Training Monitoring
problem: Catching covert distributed training during an AI pause depends on the claim that such training leaves detectable signatures, but beginners and policy analysts lack any hands-on reproducible demonstration of what those signatures look like at small scale.
direction: Using small open models (GPT-2-small or a 70M-160M Pythia model) trainable on a single consumer GPU, simulate 'normal' centralized training vs 'covert distributed' training emulated by gradient-accumulation across artificially partitioned, communication-delayed shards with staleness. Record loss curves, gradient-noise statistics, and throughput patterns, then test whether a simple classifier separates the two regimes. Deliverable: a labeled toy dataset of training-telemetry traces plus a notebook showing which features are most discriminative.
why_it_matters: Gives the governance community a concrete replicable existence proof and a starter feature set for what monitoring of compute/training telemetry might key on.
relevant_context: Extends 'Catching Illicit Distributed Training Operations During an AI Pause' (Rahman, MIRI TGT) — its assertion that covert distributed training leaves detectable signatures.
source_paper: Catching Illicit Distributed Training Operations — https://techgov.intelligence.org/blog/catching-illicit-distributed-training-operations-during-an-ai-pause

title: Do Coherence Checks Catch 'Fried' Model Organisms? A Cheap Replication on Open LoRA Adapters
problem: Daniel Tan et al. argue many emergent-misalignment model organisms are 'fried' — they lose preference coherence and instruction-following while still passing standard benchmarks — but there is no easy beginner-runnable diagnostic that flags this degradation.
direction: Take publicly released emergent-misalignment LoRA adapters (Model-Organisms-for-EM Qwen/Llama adapters) and their base models, run inference-only, and reproduce a simple 'mu-decisiveness'-style coherence metric: present forced-choice preference pairs and measure transitivity/consistency, plus an instruction-following pass rate. Compare base vs organism to quantify the coherence drop, and check whether the drop correlates with the strength of induced misalignment. Deliverable: a reproducible 'coherence health check' notebook and a table ranking which public organisms are most degraded.
why_it_matters: If widely-used model organisms are degraded proxies, downstream alignment results built on them may not transfer; a cheap standardized coherence check lets the community sanity-check organisms before trusting them.
relevant_context: Replicates and extends 'Your Model Organisms Might Be Fried' (Tan, Bostock, Africa et al.) — its mu-decisiveness coherence-drop result, as a reusable diagnostic.
source_paper: Your Model Organisms Might Be Fried — https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/WmEcgcstzYCcMpc7z/your-model-organisms-might-be-fried

title: Does Smaller-Dataset Misalignment Fry Models Less? Mapping Coherence Loss vs Fine-Tune Intensity
problem: It is unclear whether the coherence degradation in model organisms is intrinsic to inducing misalignment or an artifact of overly aggressive fine-tuning, which matters for whether 'less-fried' organisms are achievable.
direction: Using one open base model and a single public narrowly-misaligned dataset, train a series of cheap rank-1/rank-2 LoRA adapters varying only fine-tuning intensity (epochs, learning rate, dataset size). For each, measure both the induced misalignment rate and the coherence/instruction-following drop, producing a Pareto front of misalignment-achieved vs coherence-preserved. Deliverable: a plot identifying whether low-intensity fine-tunes can induce misalignment without frying, plus a recommended recipe.
why_it_matters: Tells researchers whether realistic undegraded model organisms are feasible and how to make them, improving the validity of every study that relies on such organisms.
relevant_context: Extends 'Your Model Organisms Might Be Fried' — tests its open thread on whether fixes preserve coherence via a fine-tune-intensity sweep.
source_paper: Your Model Organisms Might Be Fried — https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/WmEcgcstzYCcMpc7z/your-model-organisms-might-be-fried

title: Causal vs Correlational: Does Prompt-Steered Sycophancy Survive an Intervention Test?
problem: The position paper warns that anthropomorphic-misalignment claims often rest on correlational probes rather than causal interventions; sycophancy in particular is usually measured by correlating user-stated opinions with model agreement, which cannot rule out confounds.
direction: Build a small sycophancy benchmark on 2-3 open chat models where, for the same factual question, you causally intervene by randomly varying only the user's stated belief (correct, incorrect, none) while holding question content fixed. Measure the causal effect of the manipulated belief on answer flips, distinguishing true sycophancy from baseline error. Deliverable: a per-model 'causal sycophancy effect size' with confidence intervals and a comparison to a naive correlational metric, showing how much the correlational number overstates.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates concretely how a correlational misalignment metric can mislead and how a cheap randomized intervention fixes it — the methodological upgrade the position paper calls for, preventing over/under-stated claims from driving decisions.
relevant_context: Extends 'Position: Anthropomorphic Misalignment Research Needs Stronger Evidence' (Gupta, Krause, Tramer et al.) — implements its prescription for causal interventions over correlational probes, on sycophancy.
source_paper: Position: Anthropomorphic Misalignment Research Needs Stronger Evidence — https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07612

title: Operationalizing the Evidence-Level Checklist: Re-Scoring Three High-Profile Misalignment Results
problem: The position paper proposes graduated 'evidence levels' and a diagnostic checklist but, as a position paper, does not apply them systematically; researchers lack a worked example of scoring real published claims against the checklist.
direction: Turn the paper's proposed checklist (conceptual clarity, dataset robustness, experimental design, causal vs correlational evidence) into an explicit rubric with a 0-3 scale and anchored definitions per item. Then apply it to 3 widely-cited anthropomorphic-misalignment results (a deception, an emergent-misalignment, and a sycophancy paper), with two independent raters scoring each and inter-rater agreement reported. Deliverable: a filled scorecard plus a blog post identifying which evidentiary dimensions are systematically weakest.
why_it_matters: Converts an abstract methodological framework into a usable tested instrument and provides a public baseline of how today's headline misalignment claims actually score, raising the evidentiary bar across the field.
relevant_context: Operationalizes the open thread in 'Position: Anthropomorphic Misalignment Research Needs Stronger Evidence' to adopt graduated evidence levels and re-evaluate high-profile results against the checklist.
source_paper: Position: Anthropomorphic Misalignment Research Needs Stronger Evidence — https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07612

title: Dataset Non-Robustness: How Fragile Are Deception Benchmarks to Trivial Paraphrasing?
problem: The position paper flags 'non-robust datasets' as a key reason misalignment claims are overinterpreted, but offers no quantitative measure of how fragile existing deception/sycophancy benchmarks are to superficial rewording.
direction: Take an existing public deception-or-sycophancy benchmark, apply meaning-preserving perturbations (paraphrase, reorder options, swap entity names, change formatting) using a cheap open model or templates, and re-run 2-3 open models inference-only. Measure how much the 'misalignment rate' shifts under perturbations that should not change the correct answer. Deliverable: a robustness gap metric (variance of misalignment score across perturbations) per benchmark and the perturbation types that most destabilize results.
why_it_matters: Shows whether reported misalignment rates measure a real propensity or a brittle-prompt artifact — a precondition the position paper says must be met before claims inform high-stakes decisions.
relevant_context: Extends 'Position: Anthropomorphic Misalignment Research Needs Stronger Evidence' — operationalizes its 'non-robust datasets' failure mode into a perturbation-stability test.
source_paper: Position: Anthropomorphic Misalignment Research Needs Stronger Evidence — https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07612
